title: Taming the ox
hookLine: picture five: patient discipline, the rope kept close (Ox-Herding 5)
tomorrow: why is the herder playing a flute on the way home?

cards: New job, new gym, new anything, and the first question in your head might be: what's the secret? A monk once brought that question to the Zen teacher Zhaozhou. I've just entered the monastery, he said.
Please teach me. Zhaozhou asked: have you eaten your rice gruel? Yes, said the monk.
Then wash your bowl. That's the whole exchange. It sounds like a brush-off.
It isn't, and Zen kept it as a koan, in a collection called the Gateless Gate.

teach.b: Kuoan's fifth picture says the same thing with a rope. The preface: when one thought rises, another follows right behind it. Things don't come from outside; they come from your own mind.
So hold the nose-rope tight, and don't waver.
The verse: keep whip and rope close, or the ox will wander off into the dust. Then the turn. Well tended, the ox grows gentle, and follows of its own accord, with no need for a tether.
That's the Zen teaching about practice, named plainly: awakening isn't kept by one big moment. It's kept by daily, ordinary practice, the bowl washed every morning.
Zhaozhou didn't hand the new monk a secret, because the bowl is the secret.
In Zen, eating and cleaning are practice too, not breaks from it.
And the rope isn't a punishment. It's how the ox learns the way home. Notice the end of the verse: the rope is held close so that one day it won't be needed.
Discipline here is patient, plain and daily, and it's aiming at its own retirement.

how: In Zen, sitting, eating and cleaning are all treated as practice, done daily with attention. People on this path keep their own small daily rule, especially on busy days.

o: a festival day when oxen are blessed by monks
the moment a herder sells his ox at market
the fifth picture: daily practice, rope kept close

s: Zhaozhou answered the new monk with a long talk on awakening
he asked if he'd eaten, then said: wash your bowl.
in picture five, the tamed ox ends up following without a tether
the rope is held close so that one day it isn't needed.
The preface says our troubles come from outside us
it says things arise not from outside but from one's own mind.

games.q: your cousin wants one big 'spiritual reset' weekend a year instead of any daily practice. what does picture five say?
o: the rope works by being held daily; one weekend can't stand in for it.
one strong weekend a year is plenty, as long as it's intense.
daily practice only matters until the first big glimpse.
games.why: Kuoan's herder keeps the rope close every day until the ox follows on its own, and Zhaozhou's whole lesson was wash your bowl.

practice: If there's a cup or bowl nearby, wash it slowly, or just hold it and turn it in your hands, the way Zhaozhou's monk would after breakfast. Let the two minutes be that plain: one bowl, one rope, kept close.

wordCard.voice: Taming the ox: Kuoan's fifth picture. Patient discipline, the rope kept close until the ox walks on its own.

orig.note: Chinese: herding the ox, the title of Kuoan's fifth picture.

carryVoice: One to keep: the rope, daily and plain, held close until it isn't needed. Picture five, done.
